rationale: Table 3: Jev 1.13 decision quality (macro F1) 0.851 (composite 0.825, 4th) is below hosted chat models Gemini 3.8 Flash 0.901, GPT-5.6 Sol 0.871, GLM 5.3 0.855 but above DeepSeek V4 Pro 0.761 and Qwen3.5-4B 0.741, while open encoders Laya (0.221-0.425) and open-jev (0.350) sit near or below the surface-cue baseline (0.329).

Table 4 probes: Jev 1.13 order sensitivity 0.039, paraphrase agreement 0.926, English gap 0.009 and Kev 4B/9B 0.065/0.080 beat the only generative probed (Qwen3.5-4B order sensitivity 0.139, paraphrase 0.809), but Laya rows are highly order-sensitive (0.366-0.590) and Jev's slot signal 0.059 [0.020,0.107] hints at contamination; hosted chat models were not probed.

Table 3 calibration axis: Jev 1.13 0.706 (post-hoc T 1.1058) ties GLM 5.3 (0.706) and trails Gemini 3.8 Flash 0.806 and GPT-5.6 Sol 0.727 but beats DeepSeek V4 Pro 0.386 and Qwen3.5-4B 0.438; open typed models Laya (0.005-0.113) and open-jev (0.073) are essentially uncalibrated.

Table 3 selective-automation axis (normalised AUGRC): Jev 1.13 0.935 is level with GLM 5.3 0.936 and below Gemini 3.8 Flash 0.964 / GPT-5.6 Sol 0.943, above DeepSeek 0.862 and Qwen 0.857; open typed models range from Kev 4B 0.866 down to Laya 0.365-0.547 and open-jev 0.501.

Sec 5.1-5.3, 5.7, Tables 2-3: on three laya checkpoints the decision follows option labels not definitions (deleting definitions leaves accuracy 0.8559 vs 0.8487; contradicting labels drop it to 0.1357; A/B labels +0.1511 on PolicyBench-XF); von is label-invariant but every typed model ignores negation (flip 0.9656-0.9825, von 0.9711) vs 0.7972 for the Qwen2.5-1.5B readout, while the label effect is comparable in LM readouts (Qwen2.5-7B +0.1203, Mistral-7B +0.1531).

Table 6 (Sec 5.8): confidence AUROC for laya-td falls from 0.8123 (aligned labels) to 0.2433 under label/definition conflict (laya-en 0.8236 to 0.1940), so confidence ranks errors in the wrong direction, and negated questions return inverted answers with normal confidence (Sec 5.7); no generative confidence comparison.

Sec 5.8 and 6: under a corrupted rendering a confidence gate forwards the cases the model got right and accepts the ones it got wrong (AUROC 0.2433 for laya-td); authors advise against confidence thresholds and propose a two-rendering disagreement check instead (Table 8, laya-td precision 0.8977 at 0.8100 coverage).

Table 4 direct binary macro-F1: Jev .826/.691/.738/.960 on Dynamic/MHS/HateXplain/HateCheck vs GPT-6 Sol .897/.682/.776/.976; commercial LLMs significantly beat all decision models only on Dynamic, Decider leads MHS (.801), and open configurations vary widely (SemIf-2B .220 on MHS, Laya .655 on Dynamic) (Sec 4.1).

Sec 4.2, Fig 3: supplying the dataset definition changes 2.8%-28% of decision-model predictions with 8 significant gains and 8 losses in 28 comparisons; Jev is least sensitive (<=0.5 pt on Dynamic/HateCheck, -2.7 MHS, +3.9 HateXplain) while the policy-conditioned generative baseline CoPE loses agreement on 3 of 4 datasets and SemIf-4B swings -7.2 to +10.3.

Table 4 / Sec 4.3: decomposing the definition into per-criterion questions with a fixed rule significantly improves macro-F1 in 6/30 comparisons and lowers it in 11 (Laya -12.1 Dynamic, Decider -34.0 HateCheck; Jev +1.6 Dynamic), with no supported gain for either commercial LLM (Luna up to -6.4); components make the verdict rule inspectable but cannot show which answer is wrong (Sec 5).

Appendix I (exploratory, cached predictions): referring Laya's 20% lowest-margin texts to GPT-6 Sol raises macro-F1 .658->.729 Dynamic, .696->.721 MHS, .730->.763 HateXplain, but referring to Luna lowers HateXplain to .714; referral fraction not selected on dev data and cascade latency not measured.

Sec 4.4, Fig 5: on HateCheck Jev direct costs $0.033 per 1K texts vs $0.120 (Luna) and $1.177 (Sol), median 336 ms vs 844/1,426 ms, scoring 1.6 macro-F1 below Sol (.960 vs .976) at ~97% lower cost; Laya 48 ms but .701.

Table 1 / Sec 4.2: on 10,938 JEVal questions Jev 78.38% and InnerJev-27B 79.24% are within 3 points of GPT-6-Luna 80.93% and thinking GLM-5.3 80.37% and above non-thinking open LLMs (Qwen3.8-27B 73.81%), but trail the best generative model by 3-6 points in medicine, finance and law, and several open decision models are weak (Laya 26.30%, NanoJev 25.34%).

Table 1: Jev ECE 0.0532 and InnerJev-27B 0.0149 are below every generative configuration (best GLM-5.3-Flash high 0.0784), but Table 2/Fig 5 show Jev's full distributions are compressed (true-mode mass 89.35% vs 35.60%; prior E_mode 53.75 pp, the largest error of all configurations; posterior accuracy 67% vs 82-100% for thinking LLMs).

Sec 5.4: on SocioBench (277,500 pairs) Jev 37.69% matches non-thinking DeepSeek-V4-Flash 37.90% at 0.50 s vs 174 s per item and InnerJev-27B 39.87% vs 40.41% for thinking DeepSeek, but Jev profiling Jaccard is 53.88% vs 65.24-65.86% for Qwen3.8-27B, and in ElectionSim InnerJev-27B calls 47/51 states with vote-share errors about twice the GPT-4o-mini pipeline and every run overestimating the Democratic share by 2-6 points.

Tables 3 and 5: in-distribution SearchJev cuts mean ECE by 74.4%/40.7% vs same-size Qwen3.5 AR (JSON) after soft-label training plus fitted output-type temperatures, and Jev 1.13 has the lowest mean ECE; out-of-distribution calibration is task-dependent (SearchJev-0.8B relevance ECE 31.4 vs Qwen3.5-4B 10.6; Jev better calibrated on 3 of 4 families).

Table 4 (BrowseComp-Plus, 100 questions, single run): confidence-gated dual-system agents reach 46.0% (Jev 1.13, SearchJev-0.8B) and 54.0% (SearchJev-4B) vs 45.0% for the Qwen3.5-27B System-2-only agent with fewer System-2 calls (62.1-84.6 vs 90.3) and 868-1,102 s vs 4,080 s median active time.

Appendix B: asking each pair in both orders gives flip rates 8.8%/8.5% concentrated in low-confidence pairs (0.0000 above p=.95), position bias -0.0358/0.0030, forward vs reversed scales correlating 0.982, sparse-triplet transitivity 98.18% within the published generative-scorer range 95.95-99.06%, and test-retest winner agreement 98.6%.

Fig 2 and App. B: asked once, Jev's ECE is lower than GPT-6 Luna's token probabilities on all eight reading tasks (74% of Luna's probabilities <0.01 or >0.99 vs 18% for Jev) and its AUROC higher on 7/8, but Qwen3.8-27B has lower ECE on the four pairwise tasks (e.g. 0.011 vs 0.071 on expert pairs) and AUROC not consistently different.

Table 2: Jev is faster (0.09-0.27 s vs 0.75-1.04 s for Luna and 0.39-0.87 s for Qwen) but not cheaper than GPT-6 Luna at Batch prices (Luna cheaper on 6/7 tasks, e.g. $0.008 vs $0.018 per 1K decisions), with accuracy on par with Luna/Qwen across seven replications (Table 1), so the authors see only speed and parsing advantages.

Table 2: zero-shot CLM-v0.1-8B scores 0.351-0.593, is indistinguishable from chance on RM-Bench (0.508) and JudgeBench (0.475) and answers every HaluEval item with one label (0.581 = always-first), while generative Qwen3-8B reaches 0.611-0.778 (all gaps significant, BH q=0.05); laya is at or near chance everywhere.

Sec 4 order and length stability: CLM's order-flip rate is 0.0002 (3 exact ties) vs 0.2188 for the generative judge, and its length-preference shift is -0.023 vs -0.217, although the laya baseline flips at 0.4395 (largely truncated inputs).

Table 3: raw CLM confidence is overconfident by +0.235 to +0.401 on all six benchmarks; one pooled temperature (20.1) fit on held-out calibration items cuts ECE to 0.032-0.062, i.e. calibration only after added recalibration; calibrated confidence ranks errors above chance on 3 of 6 benchmarks (AUROC 0.587-0.609).

Table 4 (preregistered): at the 0.97 retention bar the confidence gate escalates 0.923-1.000 of items to the strong judge, retained items cost significant accuracy (-0.009 to -0.019) and random escalation at the matched fraction performs comparably; no acceptance rule reaches the 0.10 error target on 5 of 6 benchmarks.

Sec 4.1-4.4 and 5.4: menu-only interventions are predictable to within 4.2 points for seven decision-model families (exact for Open-Jev) while same-scale generative Qwen3 models err by 1.6-15.8 points, yet question wording alone moves Open-Jev-2B from 0.454 to 0.714 and putting the correct label first on a small self-selected menu drops kev-0.8B from 0.622 to 0.426.

Sec 4.2 and 5.1: pass-1 probabilities are systematically too high after a menu change (probability-level estimator errs by 21.0 points), and ECE falls from 0.09 to 0.03 only when two order-permuted passes are averaged, an added condition.

Sec 5.2, Table 2: escalating kev-0.8B's least-confident items to kev-4B beats every re-ask scheme at matched cost (0.760 at 2.40 units vs 0.652 at 2.00) and the kev gate beats random routing on four sources by 2.0-7.2 points, but the decider family's gate does not beat random on every source and authors require per-model/dataset validation.

Table 3 (PluRule test, 2,829 pairs): Jev-compact EMA 48.4-58.3 vs published GPT-5.2 54.1-57.7 and Laya 35.8-49.3; Tables 5-7: Jev F1 66.1 OLID / 65.5-65.9 HateXplain vs Detoxify <=65.7/57.0 and ModerationBench AUROC .893-.940, while Laya is near chance on ModerationBench Choice (AUROC .521) and has HateModerate NAD EMA 6.2.

Sec 4.1 (HateModerate RAD semantic vs opaque labels): human-readable policy names instead of arbitrary identifiers lower Jev-compact binary accuracy by 5.06 points (95% CI -6.21 to -3.91) and EMA by 1.64, and raise Laya's accuracy 2.5 but lower EMA 2.0, i.e. label naming shifts the operating point without improving policy application.
Table 8 / Sec 4.3: Jev confidence Brier .111-.264 with correctness AUC .628-.823, which the authors describe as not consistently calibrated; Laya confidence Brier .214-.346 with AUC only .560-.593.

Table 8: Jev decisions with confidence >=0.8 are more accurate than unfiltered (ModerationBench 94.3% at 71.9% coverage; OLID 85.5% at 54.6%) but only 67.6% at 41.0% on the PluRule test intersection, while Laya's high-confidence coverage is 2.0-19.2% with accepted accuracy 27.9-63.4%.

Sec 4.2, Fig 3 (1,000-sample estimates): Jev reaches macro-F1 0.531 on ESCI and AUROC 0.846 on RAID AI-text detection, above every bottled LLM artifact (best 0.499 and 0.822) but below zero-shot LLMs on ESCI (e.g. GLM 5.3 0.593, GPT 5.6 Terra 0.573, Sec 4.1).

Sec 4.2: Jev's projected full-workload cost ($104.89 ESCI, $223.16 RAID) is far below zero-shot LLM inference (e.g. Opus 5 $27,914 on MAVE) but above bottled artifacts that retain 94-97% of its score ($26.28 and $4.69); Jev's cost grows linearly with workload and it cannot serve generative tasks.
Appendix N: on 500 human-graded passage pairs Jev picks the same answer in both presentation orders on 94.8% vs 90.6% for Qwen3-32B, and on 80,000 training pairs 86.7% vs 72.0%.

Sec 5.5: against Stockfish preferences on 12,280 held-out chess pairs Jev has the lowest ECE, 0.081, vs 0.159 DiffusionGemma, 0.176 OLMo-2-32B and 0.260 Qwen3-32B, at similar agreement (54.5% vs 52.9-54.4%).

Sec 6 / Appendix N: sending the 25% of pairs on which Jev is least certain to Qwen3-32B loses 0.047 NDCG@10 [0.013, 0.084] to Jev alone at 80,000 answers and gives -0.007 [-0.027, 0.012] at 160,000; Qwen's labels on uncertain pairs recover only 0.004.

Table 4 / Sec 6: 126,270 chess labels cost Jev $1.97 and ~16 min API time vs 1.91 GPU-h for Qwen3-32B, and 160,000 reranking labels took ~21 min vs 5.1 GPU-h while the Jev-trained reranker matched Qwen's (NDCG@10 0.637 vs 0.630).

Table 1 / Sec 5.1: zero-shot decision models over-choose 'collect' at 1.6-1.8x chance among errors regardless of option order, and shuffling options drops Strands 0.59->0.38, Kev 9B 0.60->0.50 and Kev 4B weapons 0.97->0.62 (Clef-Flash unaffected); the generative thinker shares the collect bias without reasoning (1.8x) and less with it (1.4x).

Table 2: zero-shot ECE ranges 0.10-0.57, three of the most accurate models are under-confident (mean top probability 0.31-0.42 at 0.59-0.60 accuracy), and calibration does not predict sensitivity (AUROC 0.45-0.89; Kev 9B and Strands intervals include chance).

Table 3 / Sec 5.3-5.4: deferring the least-confident 30% to a reasoning VLM beats random deferral in proportion to actor AUROC (rank corr 0.87; +0.15 for Laya base, none for Kev 9B/Strands); with actor and rate chosen on held-out games the gain is +0.13 [0.08, 0.18] (+0.08 shuffled) but not above the thinker alone (+0.05 [-0.12, 0.11]), and in closed loop no variant reaches the exit and a fixed rule behind the same gate does as well.

Sec 4.2, Table 5: with physical features Jev's yes/no answer flags 75-99% of fault windows but also 57-94% of fault-free windows (AUROC 0.65-0.68), Qwen2.5 72B errs likewise (88-100% vs 65-100%), and after recalibration no model's detection F1 exceeds flag-every-window (0.71); diagnosis is level-dependent (Jev 37% vs Qwen 72B 46% on consistency faults, 72% vs 32% on temporal, Sec 4.1).

Sec 4.1: rewording questions changes 3-6% of Jev answers (macro-F1 <=0.02) and irrelevant fields 2-6%, but class names without descriptions change 41% (consistency-fault accuracy 71%->6%), a same-content paraphrase of descriptions changes 8-9% (context faults 13%->43%), and shuffling state fields changes 13% of RP-1312 answers with the yes/no question flagging 94% of fault-free windows.

Sec 4.4: Jev's shifted ECE 0.27-0.28 beats Qwen2.5 72B 0.43, 7B 0.60 and LightGBM 0.36 and does not rise under shift, but still needs temperature scaling (0.28->0.17), accuracy is flat above p=0.55 (stated 0.94 -> 62% right), and on unobservable faults Jev keeps p>=0.7 on 63% of windows (Sec 4.6).

Sec 4.7: 190,582 Jev requests cost US$18.69 in total (~US$0.0001 and 0.19 s per request, ~US$3.40 per unit-year at 15-min checks) vs ~2 s per window for local Qwen2.5 72B, with repeat-call agreement 97-99%.
